body.html: Antifungals destroy fungi by targeting structures that fungal cells have and human cells lack. Topical antifungals treat limited, non-recurrent superficial mycoses of skin, scalp and mucosa; systemic antifungals treat invasive (visceral or septicaemic) mycoses and extensive, recurrent or chronic superficial ones. Invasive fungal infections are a major cause of death in immunocompromised patients.

Four classes: polyenes (amphotericin B) bind ergosterol in the membrane (resistance rare); azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole) inhibit ergosterol synthesis (resistance by target change or efflux); echinocandins (caspofungin, anidulafungin, micafungin) inhibit β-D-glucan synthesis in the cell wall; pyrimidines (5-flucytosine) inhibit DNA/RNA synthesis. Choose by spectrum, concentration and diffusion at the site, and route (oral or IV). Combine to potentiate and improve diffusion, broaden the spectrum, reduce toxicity with lower doses, and prevent resistance.

Amphotericin B: broad spectrum (Aspergillus fumigatus, Mucorales, Fusarium, Candida including krusei and glabrata, Cryptococcus; not A. terreus or Scedosporium prolificans); fungicidal. Three forms: deoxycholate (Fungizone), liposomal (AmBisome), lipid complex (Abelcet). Oral bioavailability 0%; good diffusion except CSF (lipid forms better) and urine (deoxycholate better). Adverse effects: infusion reactions (fever, chills, headache, myalgia; rarely collapse, bronchospasm); renal failure rising with cumulative dose; hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia; anaemia (less erythropoietin); rarely hepatitis, torsade de pointes. Lipid forms cause fewer effects.

5-Flucytosine: Candida (not krusei) and Cryptococcus; fungistatic; always in combination; oral bioavailability 90%; good CSF and urine diffusion. Toxicity: GI (pain, pseudomembranous colitis with perforation risk), liver cytolysis, bone marrow (leucopenia, agranulocytosis, pancytopenia).

Spectrum: fluconazole covers Candida albicans and parapsilosis and Cryptococcus but not Aspergillus or C. krusei; itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole and isavuconazole cover Aspergillus; only posaconazole and isavuconazole cover Mucorales. Fungicidal on Aspergillus, fungistatic on Candida. Features: many drug interactions (liver metabolism), loading dose needed, variable serum levels, diet affects absorption. With meals (fat): itraconazole capsules, posaconazole solution; outside meals: itraconazole solution, voriconazole; no influence: fluconazole, posaconazole tablets, isavuconazole. Toxicity: hepatotoxicity (more with voriconazole), rare rash, QT prolongation (itra, posa, vori; isavuconazole shortens it); itraconazole: hypokalaemia, hypertension, leg oedema; voriconazole: visual hallucinations, neuropathy, photosensitivity and skin cancers with prolonged use.

Active on Aspergillus (fungistatic) and Candida including glabrata and krusei (fungicidal; parapsilosis less); not Cryptococcus or Mucorales. Concentration-dependent; poor CSF and urine diffusion; IV only (oral bioavailability 0%). Well tolerated: liver abnormalities, few drug interactions. Regimen choice overall rests on epidemiology, the patient, the hospital setting, the fungus, the site and safety.

Antivirals target specific viral steps, so each virus family has its own drugs: herpesviruses (HSV, VZV, CMV), hepatitis B and C, HIV and influenza. Knowing the spectrum, route, monitoring and main toxicity of each is the core of this lecture.

The human herpesviruses: HHV-1 (HSV-1), HHV-2 (HSV-2), HHV-3 (VZV), HHV-4 (EBV), HHV-5 (CMV), HHV-6, HHV-7, HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus). Nucleoside analogues must be phosphorylated to the triphosphate: acyclovir and penciclovir first by viral thymidine kinase, ganciclovir by the viral UL97 phosphotransferase; cidofovir is already monophosphorylated and foscarnet acts directly on the viral DNA polymerase.

Acyclovir: inhibits viral DNA polymerase; very active on HSV-1 and HSV-2, less on VZV, almost inactive on EBV and CMV; adapt to renal function; caution in pregnancy. Valaciclovir: better absorbed, 3 times the plasma levels of acyclovir, very active on VZV. Famciclovir: prodrug of penciclovir, active on HSV and VZV.

Ganciclovir (Cymevan; CMV and HSV): CMV retinitis in HIV, 5 mg/kg/12 h for 21 days then 5 mg/kg/day until immune recovery; transplant CMV 5 mg/kg/12 h for 21 days. Slow IV with hydration; adapt to renal function; myelotoxic (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anaemia), GI and skin effects, neuropsychological disorders; contraindicated if neutrophils under 500/mm³. Valganciclovir (Rovalcyte): oral ganciclovir, better tolerated. Foscarnet (Foscavir; CMV, HSV, VZV, EBV): 90 mg/kg/12 h IV for 14-21 days with hydration; IV only; avoid other nephrotoxins; renal failure, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, genital ulcers. Cidofovir (Vistide): half-life 65 h, spaced dosing (D1, D7, then every 14 days), broad spectrum; used when ganciclovir and foscarnet are contraindicated; given with hydration and probenecid; renal failure, uveitis.

HBV oral antivirals: tenofovir disoproxil (first line: excellent resistance profile, few renal effects, 1 pill/day, cheaper), tenofovir alafenamide (better tolerated, more expensive), entecavir (good resistance profile), second line telbivudine (neuropathy, myalgia) and adefovir (renal), lamivudine (less potent, resistance within 1-2 years). Interferons: pegylated interferon weekly SC for 12 months (flu-like symptoms, depression); interferon alpha three times weekly, now rarely used. High viral load chronic HBV → tenofovir first line.

HCV direct-acting antivirals, named by suffix: protease inhibitors -previr (grazoprevir, glecaprevir), NS5A inhibitors -asvir (daclatasvir, velpatasvir, ledipasvir), polymerase inhibitors -buvir (nucleoside: sofosbuvir; non-nucleoside: dasabuvir). In Morocco: sofosbuvir with daclatasvir or velpatasvir.

Antiretroviral classes: NRTIs (zidovudine, lamivudine, abacavir, tenofovir, emtricitabine): nucleoside analogues at the catalytic site, incorporated into viral DNA → chain termination (no 3'-OH), competitive, rather high genetic barrier. NNRTIs (nevirapine, efavirenz, etravirine, rilpivirine, doravirine): bind an allosteric site, non-competitive, low genetic barrier (one mutation can suffice). Protease inhibitors (lopinavir/ritonavir, atazanavir, darunavir). Integrase inhibitors (dolutegravir, raltegravir, bictegravir, cabotegravir, elvitegravir/cobicistat). Entry inhibitors (enfuvirtide, maraviroc).

Influenza (Orthomyxoviridae, RNA; types A, B, C; haemagglutinin for attachment, neuraminidase for release): neuraminidase inhibitors oseltamivir (oral, most used; reduces severity if started within 48 hours), zanamivir (inhaled), peramivir (IV); baloxavir marboxil blocks RNA transcription; amantadine and rimantadine (M2 channel, influenza A only) are no longer recommended because of resistance.

Antibiotics are antimicrobials from organisms (e.g. fungi) or synthesis that stop bacterial growth or kill bacteria; they treat bacterial infections and are sometimes used for prevention (antibioprophylaxis). The goals of therapy: efficacy, tolerance, minimum cost. Never prescribe them for viral infections, simple coughs and colds; prefer narrow spectrum and generics.

Classified by mechanism, structure, spectrum and side effects: β-lactams, cyclins, phenicols, aminoglycosides, macrolides, quinolones, polypeptides, glycopeptides, sulphonamides, imidazoles, rifamycins, others. Five mechanisms: inhibition of cell wall synthesis; disruption of the cell membrane; inhibition of protein synthesis (ribosome); inhibition of nucleic acid synthesis; inhibition of folate synthesis. Bactericidal drugs leave fewer than 1 survivor per 100,000 bacteria; bacteriostatic drugs stop growth and rely on the immune system.

Time-dependent antibiotics: efficacy depends on the time above the MIC (T > MIC), so divide doses, use continuous infusion and keep strict intervals: β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems), glycopeptides (vancomycin), macrolides. Concentration-dependent antibiotics: efficacy depends on the peak/MIC ratio, with a marked post-antibiotic effect, so give a single high daily dose: aminoglycosides (amikacin, gentamicin) and fluoroquinolones.

Germ: empiric choice from the usual organisms at the site (urinary tract infection → Gram-negative bacilli) and the place of acquisition (community vs hospital), then adapt to the isolated germ and its susceptibility. Site: tissue diffusion, renal or biliary elimination, intracellular diffusion for intracellular germs (Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Legionella). Resistance: usually susceptible (group A β-haemolytic streptococcus), increasing (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae), multiresistant (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter). Host: extremes of age, pregnancy (faster clearance; teratogenic or toxic drugs), lactation, renal or hepatic dysfunction (lower doses or longer intervals), allergy or intolerance.

Pregnancy: penicillins and cephalosporins are safe; avoid cyclins, aminoglycosides, quinolones and high-dose metronidazole.

Oral for mild-moderate infections with normal gut function; parenteral (IV more than IM) for poorly absorbed drugs (aminoglycosides), serious infections or when oral is impossible (vomiting, coma). Number of doses depends on PK/PD, route and severity; start directly at the needed dose. Duration depends on the germ, the site (bone, CSF), host (neutropenia) and complications, with a trend toward shorter courses.

Monotherapy is preferred. Combine for synergy (septicaemia, endocarditis, listeriosis, nosocomial infections, brucellosis), for empiric therapy in critically ill patients, to widen the spectrum in polymicrobial infections, and to prevent resistance (tuberculosis; staphylococci treated with a quinolone).

Response: clinical (fever, tachycardia and confusion fall, local signs disappear, no relapse after stopping), laboratory (falling white count and CRP, negative cultures), imaging, and watch for side effects. Fighting resistance: patients use antibiotics only when prescribed, complete the course and never share them; health workers improve infection control and prescribe and dispense only when truly needed and the right drug; policy-makers strengthen surveillance and laboratories and regulate use.

Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal infection caused by Vibrio cholerae, responsible for epidemics and pandemics where drinking water and sanitation are lacking. It is a notifiable disease. Death comes from dehydration, and rehydration saves lives.

V. cholerae is a Gram-negative, facultatively aerobic, comma-shaped rod with a polar flagellum. The cholera toxin (CTX) is the main virulence factor: it disrupts normal fluid reabsorption and causes a massive secretory diarrhoea that can reach 15 litres per day, leading to dehydration.
Faecal-oral, mainly through contaminated water or food. Endemic in parts of Africa, Asia and Latin America; linked to poor hygiene, humanitarian crises, natural disasters and wars.

Incubation a few hours to 5 days. Typical cholera: profuse watery 'rice-water' stools, no fever, vomiting, muscle cramps and severe dehydration (hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria, skin fold, altered consciousness). Without prompt treatment: hypovolaemic shock and acute renal failure.

Diagnosis: clinical picture in an epidemic context, confirmed by stool culture on TCBS selective medium; rapid antigen tests (less sensitive); PCR for virulence genes. Treatment: rehydration is the cornerstone (oral rehydration salts for moderate cases, IV Ringer lactate for severe dehydration); antibiotics shorten symptoms and shedding: single-dose doxycycline first line, alternatives azithromycin (children) and ciprofloxacin. Prevention: safe water, sanitation, hand washing; inactivated oral cholera vaccines (Dukoral, Shanchol, Euvichol) in endemic areas and outbreaks; surveillance and rapid response.

Beyond Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis, AIDS brings a set of infections and cancers that should each prompt HIV screening: oro-oesophageal candidiasis, tuberculosis, CMV infection, cryptosporidiosis, Kaposi sarcoma and lymphomas.
Bucco-oesophageal candidiasis in a person living with HIV: dysphagia, retrosternal pain and a whitish oropharyngeal coating. Confirm with upper GI endoscopy; treat with fluconazole; screen for HIV.

The most frequent opportunistic infection in AIDS, at all stages of immunodepression, responsible for about one third of HIV deaths. HIV raises TB risk (loss of Th1 cells, less interferon-γ); TB accelerates HIV (macrophages make TNF, IL-1 and IL-6, increasing replication). With moderate immunodepression TB looks as in immunocompetent people; with severe immunodepression forms are more extensive and severe, resistant bacilli emerge and drug side effects are commoner. Diagnosis: find the bacillus (BK), plus clinical, biological and radiological clues. Rule: every TB patient is screened for HIV, and every HIV patient is assessed for TB.

CMV appears at CD4 under 50/mm³. Retinitis is the main site: visual problems, fundus with exudates and haemorrhagic necrosis, risk of blindness. Extra-retinal: colitis, oesophagitis, gastritis, cholangitis, encephalitis, myelitis, neuropathy, pneumonia. Chronic diarrhoea in AIDS: cryptosporidiosis, isosporiasis. Cryptosporidiosis: intestinal (acute or chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain) or biliary (sclerosing cholangitis, pain, vomiting); diagnosed by stool parasitology, colonoscopic biopsy and abdominal ultrasound.

HIV does not directly cause cancer but promotes it through immunosuppression; the cancers are due to other viruses: HHV-8 → Kaposi sarcoma, EBV → non-Hodgkin lymphoma, HPV → cervical cancer. All are AIDS indicators and require HIV screening. Kaposi sarcoma: skin, mucosal and/or visceral; lesions are purple-brown macules, pigmented papulo-nodules, angiomatoid nodules, infiltrated, verrucous or ulcerated plaques; limb lymphoedema can reveal it; many lesions, mucosal and facial locations are suggestive; biopsy confirms. Lymphomas are staged with CT and MRI.

HIV progressively destroys the immune system. Before antiretroviral therapy (ART) it was fatal; with ART it is a chronic, slowly progressive disease with near-normal life expectancy, but there is no cure and no vaccine, and treatment is lifelong. Diagnosis is often late because symptoms are varied and the subject is hard to raise; management is multidisciplinary and prevention matters at every stage.

HIV-1 is worldwide; HIV-2 mostly West Africa. Main target: CD4+ T lymphocytes (90% of infected cells; high-affinity receptor), also brain glial cells. CD4 destruction causes immunosuppression and AIDS; the CD4 count measures immunodepression and ART efficacy. Late diagnosis means high morbidity and mortality and continued transmission. Worldwide about 40.8 million people live with HIV (end 2024), two thirds in Africa. In Morocco national prevalence is about 0.08%, a concentrated epidemic in key populations (people who inject drugs, sex workers, men who have sex with men), with mainly heterosexual transmission; the 25-44 age group is most affected.

Routes: sexual, blood, mother-to-child. Prevention: abstinence, fidelity, condoms, PrEP (tenofovir/emtricitabine) for HIV-negative adults over 18, HBV-vaccinated, with regular risk: 1 tablet daily, continued until 2 days after the last intercourse; it does not protect against other STIs or hepatitis C. Post-exposure prophylaxis: triple therapy as soon as possible, ideally within 4 h and no later than 48-72 h, for 4 weeks. Mother-to-child transmission (pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding): 25-40% without treatment, under 1% with maternal ARVs, no breastfeeding, delivery mode adapted to viral load, and ARV syrup for the newborn for 1 month. Wanting a child is a legitimate right: plan the pregnancy and screen at every stage.

Screening: fourth-generation ELISA (antibodies + p24 antigen, shorter window) or a rapid test (TROD) on serum, plasma or whole blood in under 30 minutes; saliva self-tests exist in some pharmacies. Confirmation: plasma viral load; Western blot only for discordant cases (positive screen, undetectable load: HIV-2, elite controllers). Testing follows the 5 Cs: consent, counselling, confidentiality, correct results, connection to care; offered, never imposed or done without the patient's knowledge. Occasions: symptoms, voluntary or systematic screening (pregnancy, STI, premarital, blood donation, rape).

Suggestive signs: weight loss, oral candidiasis, diarrhoea over a month, prolonged fever, prurigo, generalised lymphadenopathy, multi-dermatome or recurrent shingles, severe bacterial infections, seborrhoeic dermatitis, recurrent vaginal candidiasis, neuropathy; clues are chronicity, unusual presentation (extensive shingles in a young person) and failure of usual treatment.

Opportunistic infections: tuberculosis, Pneumocystis pneumonia, cerebral toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis, oesophageal candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis, lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, cryptosporidiosis, HIV encephalitis. They appear as CD4 fall: candidiasis, TB and Kaposi first; Pneumocystis and toxoplasmosis around 200; cryptococcosis, CMV and lymphomas around 100. The CD4 count predicts infections, times prophylaxis and assesses ART. CDC categories: A primary or asymptomatic infection, B minor infections, weight loss, asthenia, C opportunistic infections, tumours, encephalopathy.

Management combines counselling, treatment of opportunistic infections and tumours, prophylaxis and ART. ARV targets: reverse transcriptase (NRTI, NNRTI), protease, integrase, attachment/fusion. Goals: sustained undetectable viral load, restored CD4 count, better health and quality of life, and reduced transmission. Regimen: 2 NRTIs + 1 NNRTI, or 1 protease inhibitor, or 1 integrase inhibitor: at least three drugs, without interruption, for life (the integrated provirus persists), with strict adherence and attention to interactions and comorbidities. To do no harm: initial clinical and biological assessment, immunovirological monitoring, adherence support.

Leptospirosis is a zoonosis caused by spirochetes of the genus Leptospira. WHO estimates 873,000 cases and over 40,000 deaths a year. In Morocco the commonest human serotype is L. icterohaemorrhagiae. Severe (icteric) forms combine fever, jaundice, renal failure and haemorrhage and often need resuscitation.

Two species: L. biflexa (saprophytic) and L. interrogans (pathogenic; 230 serovars in 23 serogroups): icterohaemorrhagiae, canicola, pomona, grippotyphosa, australis. Reservoir: rodents (rats, mice) and domestic animals (dogs, pigs). Humans are infected through animal urine, contaminated water or soil (public baths) or infected tissue, entering via cuts, abraded skin, mucous membranes or conjunctivae. At-risk jobs: slaughterhouse workers, miners, sewer workers, garbage collectors; often an occupational disease.

Anicteric (self-limited): sudden flu-like illness with fever, rigors, headache, cough, myalgia, non-itchy rash, anorexia, diarrhoea; lasts a few days, rarely fatal; may recur days later in the immune stage with aseptic meningitis. Icteric (severe): fever, renal failure, jaundice, haemorrhage, respiratory distress, with possible heart, CNS and muscle involvement; may last weeks or months in survivors.

Direct detection: dark-field microscopy (blood, urine) and culture (slow, special media). PCR: positive in blood from day 1. Serology on two samples 15 days apart (late seroconversion is common): ELISA IgM from day 8 (positive > 1/400); microscopic agglutination test (MAT, Martin and Pettit), the reference method, positive from day 10 (> 1/100); rapid strip tests.

Antibiotics: penicillin G 100,000 IU/kg/day or amoxicillin 100 mg/kg/day for 10 days, or ceftriaxone 2 g/day for 7-10 days, or doxycycline 200 mg/day for 7 days. Supportive care: fluids and forced diuresis if renal failure with preserved urine output, transfusion for haemorrhage, haemodialysis for renal failure, treatment of cardiovascular collapse, ventilation if consciousness is impaired; severe forms are often fatal without resuscitation. Prevention: rodent control (especially public baths), bathing hygiene, individual protection (gloves, boots, glasses, covering wounds) and vaccination for occupational risk (sewer workers, garbage collectors).

Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges (bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic or non-infectious) and is a medical emergency because of the nearby brain and spinal cord. Bacteria enter the bloodstream, cross the blood-brain barrier, multiply in the CSF and trigger inflammation. Meningeal syndrome + fever = meningitis until proven otherwise; in adults the main bacteria are pneumococcus and meningococcus, and first-line treatment is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime.

Adults: Neisseria meningitidis (Gram-negative diplococcus), Streptococcus pneumoniae (Gram-positive), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast, Ziehl-Neelsen, Löwenstein-Jensen culture). Newborns up to 3 months: group B streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes, TB. Older children: meningococcus, pneumococcus, H. influenzae type b, TB. Listeria (Gram-positive) grows at refrigerator temperature and is carried by milk, cheese, eggs, ice cream, poultry, raw meat and smoked fish.

Meningeal syndrome: headache, vomiting, nuchal rigidity (cannot flex the neck), photophobia, with fever. Brudzinski's sign: passive neck flexion causes hip and knee flexion; Kernig's sign: pain and resistance extending the knee with the hip flexed. Severity signs: extensive purpura, neurological deficit, coma, shock. Differential: bacterial (including partially treated 'decapitated') and tuberculous meningitis, viral or fungal meningitis, brain abscess.

LP follows a neurological examination but must never delay antibiotics. Contraindications: skin sepsis at the site, bleeding coagulopathy, raised intracranial pressure or suspected intracranial mass (risk of herniation), assessed by fundus (papilloedema) and CT (midline shift, mass, diffuse oedema). Collect 2-3 tubes (cytology/bacteriology, chemistry). Normal CSF: under 3 cells/mm³, protein under 0.4 g/L, CSF/serum glucose 0.5. Meningococcal/pneumococcal: turbid, ≥ 1,000 cells, neutrophils, high protein, low glucose. Tuberculous and Listeria: clear, lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose. Viral: under 100 lymphocytes, normal glucose. Bloody CSF: three-tube method: clearing with clots = traumatic tap; no clearing, no clot = intracranial haemorrhage.

Meningococcal: sporadic or epidemic (schools); report immediately by phone; nasopharyngeal saprophyte spread by droplets; sudden, frank meningeal syndrome; purpura is very suggestive and, if extensive (purpura fulminans), highly lethal. Pneumococcal: entry via otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia; sudden onset; high mortality. Tuberculous: progressive onset, fever around 38 °C, weight loss, asthenia, seizures, mental changes; meningeal syndrome + oculomotor palsy is very suggestive; clear lymphocytic CSF, protein over 1 g/L, low glucose; hyponatraemia; complications: hydrocephalus, palsies, epilepsy. Listeria: pregnancy, alcoholism, immunodeficiency, steroids (20% with no risk factor); meningeal syndrome with cranial nerve palsies.

Pneumococcal/meningococcal: ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day or cefotaxime 200-300 mg/kg/day IV, 10-14 days for pneumococcus, 7 days for meningococcus. Tuberculous: 2 RHZE / 7 RH plus corticosteroids. Listeria: amoxicillin 200 mg/kg/day + gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day for 2-3 weeks. Meningococcal prophylaxis of contacts: rifampicin 600 mg twice daily for 2 days (preferred), or spiramycin, ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin; plus meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccination.

A prolonged (persistent) fever is a temperature above 38.3 °C, observed repeatedly, for 3 weeks, without an obvious cause after a clinical examination and routine tests. It is a common reason for consultation and admission and a diagnostic challenge: blind antibiotics breed resistance and delay the diagnosis, and about 25% of cases remain undiagnosed. The approach is careful history and repeated examination, then tests from simple to complex in two waves.

Four families (plus a fifth: no diagnosis). 1. Infections (20-25% in Western countries; tuberculosis is the first cause in developing countries): systemic bacterial (extrapulmonary or miliary TB, typhoid, endocarditis, bacteraemia), deep suppurations (abdominal abscesses, osteomyelitis, spondylodiscitis), focal infections (dental, ENT, hepatobiliary, urogenital); parasitic (malaria, visceral leishmaniasis, toxoplasmosis, hepatic amoebiasis, schistosomiasis); viral (CMV, EBV, HIV); fungal (candidiasis, cryptococcosis, aspergillosis). 2. Systemic inflammatory diseases (25-30%): Horton disease (elderly; temporal artery biopsy), Still disease (young adult; polyarthralgia, fleeting rash, leukocytosis, cytolysis), lupus, IBD, granulomatoses and vasculitides. 3. Neoplasms: lymphomas, leukaemias, solid tumours (kidney, digestive tract, liver, ovary, pancreas, prostate, lung, thyroid). 4. Miscellaneous: thromboembolism, deep haematoma; drug fever (β-lactams, sulphonamides, α-methyldopa, carbamazepine, phenytoin, bleomycin, progestogens); hyperthyroidism, thyroiditis, phaeochromocytoma; autonomic thermal dysregulation; factitious fever (high temperature without tachycardia and normal tests; thermometer manipulation or self-injection of pyrogens).

Fever: date and mode of onset, temperature curve, circumstances. Accompanying signs: tachycardia, chills, sweats, weight loss, arthralgia, skin, digestive, respiratory, urinary, neurological signs. Context: age (elderly: Horton and tumours); occupation (vet: brucellosis; sewer worker: leptospirosis; butcher: toxoplasmosis; health worker: HBV, HCV, HIV, TB); origin and travel (TB, malaria; fresh-water swimming: leptospirosis, schistosomiasis); food (raw fish or plants: distomatosis; unpasteurised dairy: brucellosis); animals (rat urine: leptospirosis; dog ticks: rickettsiosis); history (TB contact, prosthesis, valve disease, previous episodes); cancer risk (tobacco, alcohol, asbestos, hepatitis). Examination: methodical, thorough, repeated daily; confirm the fever is real; examine chest, abdomen, pelvis, skin and mucosa, nodes, palpable arteries, nervous and osteoarticular systems. Decide: well tolerated with preserved state → outpatient; admit if neutropenic, splenectomised, valvular disease, cancer, cirrhosis, immunocompromised, HIV with CD4 under 200, or prosthesis.

First wave (minimally invasive): CBC and platelets; at least 3 blood cultures; urine culture, dipstick, 24-h proteinuria; CRP, ESR, fibrinogen, protein electrophoresis; ionogram, renal and liver tests, glucose, calcium, CPK, LDH, coagulation; chest X-ray; tuberculin test and TB search in sputum and urine; serologies (brucellosis (Wright), typhoid (Widal-Felix), leptospirosis (Martin-Pettit), rickettsiosis, CMV, HIV, EBV, hepatitis, toxoplasmosis, leishmaniasis); thick blood smear; sinus and dental X-rays; abdominopelvic ultrasound; antinuclear antibodies; TSH, T4. Reading the CBC: marked leukocytosis (suppuration, septicaemia, Hodgkin); normal or low (salmonella, TB, brucellosis, viruses); lymphopenia (HIV, lupus); hypereosinophilia (parasites, allergy); mononucleosis syndrome (EBV, toxoplasmosis, CMV).

Second wave (invasive, costly): special blood cultures; lumbar puncture; echocardiography (systematic even without a murmur); arterial and venous ultrasound; CT abdomen and chest; endoscopies; bronchoscopy; bone scintigraphy; brain MRI and angiography; punctures and biopsies (temporal artery biopsy in elderly patients).

Rabies is a viral zoonosis of domestic and wild animals causing an encephalomyelitis that is always fatal once symptoms appear. There is no curative treatment: only prevention works, made possible by the long incubation.

Spread by saliva: bites, scratches, licking of broken skin or mucous membranes. Human-to-human transmission is known only through corneal transplants (and in theory bites, though human saliva is poorly virulent and no such case has been reported). In Morocco: 54% under 20 years, 73% male, 79% rural; the biting animal is a dog in 89% and a cat in 5%.

The virus migrates along peripheral nerves to the spinal ganglion and then the CNS, where it prefers the rhinencephalon (making animals bite furiously), replicates, and spreads centrifugally along nerves to organs including the salivary glands.

Incubation: silent, 20-60 days on average (15 days to 1 year), shorter in children and with deep, multiple bites close to the nervous system. This long delay lets vaccination create immunity before disease appears. Prodrome: tingling or itching at the bite (50-80%), myoclonus, anxiety, insomnia, logorrhoea, fever, digestive signs. State phase: furious rabies (frequent): agitation, screaming, spitting, biting, hallucinations, skin and sensory hyperaesthesia, aerophobia and hydrophobia (unable to drink, agitation at the sight of water or a draught), dysautonomia (fever, sweating, irregular breathing), with normal consciousness; or paralytic rabies (less frequent): ascending flaccid paralysis, bulbar involvement. Always fatal within 3-6 days from spasm or cardiorespiratory arrest.

Permanent measures: health education; vaccination of domestic animals, capture and removal of stray dogs and cats, border control of pet imports. After exposure: clean the wound immediately (the simplest and most useful act, even hours or days later); assess severity at an anti-rabies centre; vaccination ± specific immunoglobulins (sero-vaccination). Observe the biting animal: it can shed virus in saliva before signs appear (about 1 day for cats, 3 days (1-7) for dogs); if it stays healthy, that is reassuring; if it falls ill, its brain is examined. Treat all stray animals as potentially infected.

Mediterranean spotted fever (boutonneuse fever) is a bacterial disease caused by Rickettsia conorii, transmitted by the brown dog tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus, which is both vector and reservoir. Diagnosis is clinical first: the triad fever + rash + black eschar, treated with doxycycline.

Very common around the Mediterranean for ecological reasons that favour the tick. Seasonal: summer, July to September in Morocco (immature stages develop in summer). Contact with dogs plays an important role. The adult tick bite is painless (anaesthetic, anticoagulant saliva) and the tick must feed at least 20 hours to transmit; bites are often in the armpits, groin, skin folds and genital area.

Infectious syndrome: abrupt fever to 39.5 °C, flu-like illness, headache, sometimes prostration. Rash: maculopapular, sometimes pustular, starting on the trunk; the slide states that it does not involve the palms and soles (classic descriptions of this disease include them, so check this point with your professor). Inoculation eschar ('tache noire'): a black spot at the bite site in 80%, the pathognomonic sign. Complicated forms (6-7%): purpuric rash (legs), jaundice, hepatomegaly, confusion, seizures, coma, renal failure, venous thrombosis, GI haemorrhage, arrhythmias, vasculitis; risk factors: age over 60, diabetes, alcoholism, smoking, immunosuppression, G6PD deficiency.

Diagnosis is clinical before any test (the triad). Indirect: immunofluorescence IgG and IgM, titre ≥ 1/128 or a rise 15 days apart, IgM positivity confirming; Western blot. Direct: from blood (heparinised tube or blood culture) or skin biopsy of the eschar: isolation, PCR. Non-specific findings: low platelets, low sodium and calcium, raised transaminases. Treatment: doxycycline 200 mg/day for 5-7 days or until 2 days after the fever resolves; josamycin for newborns, children and pregnant women (3 g/day for 5 days in pregnancy). Prevention: repellents, remove ticks before 20 hours of attachment, hygiene, control of stray dogs, anti-tick collars.

A collective foodborne toxi-infection (TIAC) is at least two grouped cases with similar, usually digestive (gastroenteritis) symptoms, linked to the same food. It is a notifiable disease. The causes are essentially bacterial; the incubation period and the presence of fever point to the germ.

Look at the food (undercooked, prepared the day before, badly refrigerated, raw meat or poultry, raw milk, untreated water), the incubation and the symptoms: dysenteric (mucus, blood, fever), choleriform, or extra-digestive (neurological). Short incubation (under 12 h), no fever: preformed toxins: Staphylococcus aureus (2-4 h; vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea without fever; milk and dairy, dishes prepared the day before) and Bacillus cereus. Clostridium perfringens: isolated diarrhoea without fever, from dishes prepared the day before, inadequate refrigeration, collective catering. Longer incubation (over 12 h), with fever: Salmonella (12-24 h; acute febrile diarrhoea; undercooked or raw meat, poultry, eggs, seafood), Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia (48-72 h; acute febrile diarrhoea; undercooked or raw food).

Individual: assess dehydration; stool culture and toxin testing. Rehydration is the priority; antipyretics for fever; continue or resume feeding early, avoiding stimulating foods (raw vegetables, fruit, dairy); antisecretory agents; digestive dressings of unproven value; avoid transit slowers (opioids, anticholinergics), which are contraindicated in invasive diarrhoea. Antibiotics are not systematic: only for symptoms beyond 48-72 h, suspected salmonellosis, bacterial dysentery, cholera, or risk factors (infants, elderly, immunocompromised, valve disease); options by germ: fluoroquinolones, azithromycin, cotrimoxazole. Admit for major digestive intolerance or weight loss with risk factors.

Collective: mandatory reporting; epidemiological investigation to identify and remove the responsible food and the faulty procedures; search for carriers among kitchen staff (stool culture, nose and throat swabs).

Cleaning: hand washing; utensils in hot soapy water; surfaces with disinfectant or diluted bleach. Avoid cross-contamination: never put cooked food on a plate that held raw meat, poultry, eggs, fish or seafood. Refrigeration: refrigerate or freeze perishables; do not leave prepared dishes or leftovers more than 2 hours unrefrigerated; fridge below 4.5 °C. Cook eggs and meat thoroughly.
